passage_changes.passage: The Supreme Court of the United States has struck down a set of tariffs that President Donald Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, commonly called IEEPA. The Court's decision was a 6-3 verdict. Chief Justice John Roberts clarified that IEEPA does not allow a President to take unilateral tariff actions without approval from Congress. In his reasoning, the word 'regulate' in IEEPA does not mean 'tax'. The Court observed that IEEPA was designed for emergency economic restrictions, not for general tariff policy. As a result, the Liberation Day tariffs, introduced through an executive order dated 2 April 2025, were invalidated. Before this order, no American President had used IEEPA as a means to impose trade tariffs. The judgment has also raised questions about whether tariffs already collected can be refunded. It has further raised questions about the direction of future American trade policy. Indian exporters are among those affected, since the Liberation Day tariffs had applied to many of their goods. Any broad tariff measure now needs authorisation from Congress, which places a limit on the use of emergency powers for trade protectionism. This is why the verdict is widely discussed in the context of future trade policy.

Union Budget 2026-27 places manufacturing and infrastructure at the centre of the government's growth plan. The budget describes a push to scale up production in several strategic sectors and to revive older industrial sectors so that they become more productive and competitive. Among the sectors named are biopharmaceuticals, electronics, semiconductors and critical minerals. A biopharma scheme called SHAKTI is meant to strengthen domestic production of advanced medicines, while the semiconductor programme is expected to move from assembly toward higher-value manufacturing and home-grown intellectual property. A separate scheme is planned to build a domestic container manufacturing base. The plan also addresses heavy industries whose emissions are hard to cut, and it funds technologies that capture carbon for those sectors. On infrastructure, the budget proposes new freight and rail links, along with city-to-city connectors meant to speed up movement between major urban centres. Medium-sized businesses with strong growth potential are another focus, and a dedicated fund is planned to help them compete globally. Finally, the budget plans to map cities according to their economic strengths so that each region can pursue its own growth drivers. The budget presents these measures as part of a broader blueprint for economic growth that puts young people at its centre.

A price index is useful only when it reflects what people actually buy. An economy changes over time, and so do the habits of households. Consumer spending has become more varied, cities have grown, and many purchases now happen digitally. Services now make up a larger part of household budgets, and families in towns and villages often buy different things. A consumer price index that keeps an old set of items and weights can therefore give a distorted picture of living costs. The statistical agency that compiles the index must periodically revisit the base year, the basket of goods and services, and the weights given to each item. The new base year is chosen with care, using evidence from a recent household expenditure survey and from an advisory committee of experts. Revising the index is a technical task, but its effects are practical. Pay revisions, pension adjustments and policy decisions can all depend on the index. If the index does not match real price changes, these payments and decisions may be wrong. A credible revision therefore reflects how far household money goes.

India hosted the India AI Impact Summit 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, and the event marked an important step for the Global South in artificial intelligence governance. The summit's central outcome is the New Delhi Declaration on AI, which focuses on AI that is inclusive, ethical and oriented to development. Rather than limiting the discussion to risks alone, the declaration asks how AI can deliver practical benefits to ordinary people. Its framework is organised into seven pillars, and each pillar is backed by voluntary global initiatives. Some pillars concern sharing solutions, some concern shared tools and standards, and others concern workforce preparation and energy-efficient systems. Alongside it, a separate voluntary framework for frontier AI developers was launched, with a focus on equitable access and real-world understanding of how AI is used. The theme of the gathering, welfare for all, shaped many of its discussions and gave a human focus to technical debates. Together, these efforts seek to translate high-level global discussions into outcomes that can be measured in development terms. Participants were encouraged to build scalable applications that complement national programmes, so that AI benefits reach more communities across the world.

The Great Nicobar Mega Infrastructure Project has returned to the spotlight after the National Green Tribunal upheld its Environmental Clearance. The Tribunal found that the project complied with the coastal norms that apply to the island. Great Nicobar is the largest island of the Nicobar group and sits at the southern end of India, where a dense green cover of trees meets long coastlines. Planners see the project as a major step in building trade and strategic capacity near the Malacca Strait. Critics, however, have questioned whether the damage to the island's fragile ecology can be offset. The island is also home to tribal communities. This debate highlights a familiar challenge in India: how to balance national economic and strategic goals with the protection of ecologically sensitive regions and their people. Understanding the project therefore requires knowing about the island's location, its ecology, the people who live there and the legal bodies that review such proposals. Local residents and planners will need to show how the development protects both the forest cover and the people who depend on it.

February 2026 brought several developments in India's defence sector. The Agni-III missile was successfully tested, a step that strengthens the country's strategic deterrence and its capacity for long-range strikes. The missile belongs to the ballistic class. Long-range capability is central to any deterrence policy.

Alongside missiles, engine development also drew attention. Progress on the Kaveri Engine Programme was reviewed at a research establishment, with the aim of strengthening indigenous military aviation capability. The review focused on progress made so far. The programme is part of India's Aatmanirbhar Bharat push in defence technology and seeks an indigenous jet engine for fighter aircraft.

On the global stage, the World Defence Show 2026 was held as a major international exhibition. The event showcased innovations across the defence sector. Its exhibits covered new technologies. Such events give officials and industry leaders a shared space to compare new systems.

Together, these developments show how missile testing, engine research and international showcases fit into the wider defence agenda. Each one links a technology to a national goal, and this link is worth remembering.

Union Budget 2026-27 pairs tax simplification with a cautious fiscal stance. The government decided to replace the old income tax law with a shorter statute, with the aim of reducing disputes between taxpayers and the tax department. Importantly, the existing income tax slabs were kept unchanged, so individuals did not face a change in rates for the year. Tax collected at source was also rationalised by removing thresholds for families travelling or studying abroad. Remittances for education, medical care and overseas tours were brought under a single simpler rule. A change was also proposed for companies that report high book profits but pay little or no taxable income. Under the proposal, a minimum tax would become a final tax at a lower rate than before, and non-residents would be exempted from it. On the economic side, the budget projects a growth path that combines price growth with real output growth. The government has also set a deficit target for the year and expects public debt, measured against the size of the economy, to fall gradually. A new fiscal plan aims to stabilise that debt ratio by the end of the decade. Capital spending receives special attention because infrastructure investment is seen as a strong multiplier of economic activity. Taken together, these measures seek to combine a stable tax regime with disciplined public finances.

A consumer price index tracks the prices of a fixed set of goods and services, called the basket, and gives each item a weight. When the index is revised to a new base year, the basket is reviewed so that it matches what households now buy. Several parts of the method change in such a revision. The number of items in the basket can rise, and the split between goods and services can shift to give services a larger place. Prices from online sellers may be recorded directly where the market is large enough to be tracked. The grouping of items into divisions, groups and classes follows an international classification standard, and the newer version is adopted in the revision. Housing is handled separately, through a rent index that depends on what households pay for accommodation. Coverage of this rent index can be widened beyond its earlier scope. The weight given to food is also revised, because household spending has diversified. Finally, the agency decides how widely the results are published. Each of these choices affects how accurately the index measures the cost of living.

The Great Nicobar project has raised serious environmental and social concerns. Clearing large stretches of dense forest would remove habitat for wildlife and disturb an ecosystem that has developed over long periods. Critics argue that the environmental study relied on too little field data, so it may not capture how the island's species behave across changing conditions. Compensatory afforestation has been proposed in a different state, but critics say a new plantation cannot reproduce the unique structure and species of a natural forest. Indigenous communities are at the centre of the debate. Certain tribal groups are considered especially vulnerable. Any disturbance could cause loss of habitat, disruption of traditions and a hit to local livelihoods. The island is also exposed to natural hazards. Earthquakes, tsunamis and the impacts of climate change add to concerns about building large facilities there. Supporters point to strategic and economic gains, but the debate shows how difficult it is to weigh development against ecological and tribal rights. Whether the project proceeds responsibly will depend on how well the safeguards are enforced in practice. Supporters and critics alike agree that the island's natural and human heritage needs careful protection. Clear rules on monitoring and accountability would help build trust among the communities that are most affected.

India's wetland policy combines conservation with tourism and local livelihoods. Under one capacity building scheme, a tourism ministry works with the environment ministry to make better use of wetlands. The scheme aims to enhance biodiversity, carbon stock, eco-tourism opportunities and income for local communities. Its primary focus is a shift from crowded visits to higher-value nature tourism at ecologically sensitive wetlands. Conservation at the national level is carried out through state-level bodies. A national atlas of decadal wetland change documents how these wetlands have changed over time, and an original version of that atlas was released by a national space agency unit. Such records help authorities see which wetlands have altered over a decade. Tourism is also being planned along cultural routes. A new corridor will connect Ayodhya with another place in the same state, combining cultural visits with nature, and the corridor is announced as a new route in the state. Cities are recognised too. Wetland City Accreditation is granted only to cities that satisfy all six international criteria, including measures for conservation of wetlands and their ecosystem services. The programme aims to promote conservation and wise use of urban and peri-urban wetlands.

India is investing in science, space and maritime cooperation at several levels. A new fund under the Anusandhan National Research Foundation is designed to carry research from the laboratory to industrial-scale manufacturing. Its focus areas include biotechnology, artificial intelligence, deep tech and advanced manufacturing, and it is meant to reduce import dependence. In space, the Union Budget has approved two major telescope projects in Ladakh, a region chosen for its high altitude, clear skies and minimal light pollution. One project will study the Sun, including solar magnetism and space weather, while the other will look at exoplanets, the early universe and galaxy evolution. Maritime security is also addressed through the Combined Maritime Forces, a voluntary multinational partnership headquartered in Manama, Bahrain that aims to protect sea lanes and prevent piracy and smuggling. India has taken on a larger role in this partnership by commanding one of its task forces for the first time, with a focus on training and capacity building. Together, these developments show how India links research, infrastructure and security. Such schemes are meant to strengthen domestic capability, support new industries and reduce dependence on imports in strategic sectors.

facts.title: Fiscal Discipline and Local Bodies
facts.summary: The Commission recommends that the Centre's fiscal deficit fall to 3.5 per cent of GDP and the States' limit be set at 3 per cent of GSDP by 2030-31. It also recommends ending off-budget borrowings by States and performance-linked grants for local bodies. For urban areas it proposes an urbanisation premium and a constitutional change regarding State Finance Commission recommendations.
facts: Centre's fiscal deficit to be reduced to 3.5% of GDP by 2030-31
States' fiscal deficit limit set at 3% of GSDP by 2030-31
Exclusion clause: SASCI borrowings excluded from the deficit limit
Recommends ending off-budget borrowings by States to enhance fiscal transparency
Grants to rural and urban local bodies
Performance-linked grants to rural and urban local bodies improve accountability
Urbanisation premium of 10,000 crore to merge peri-urban villages into ULBs above 1 lakh population
Special infrastructure grants of 56,100 crore for wastewater in medium-sized cities (10-50 lakh population)
Suggested removal of the requirement that Central FC recommendations be made 'on basis of' State FC recommendations
Urged DISCOM reforms including privatisation, and targeted subsidies with sunset clauses

facts.title: National Green Tribunal
facts.summary: The National Green Tribunal is a specialised environmental tribunal set up under the National Green Tribunal Act (2010), and India is the third country after Australia and New Zealand to do so. It provides relief and compensation for environmental damage, applying the polluter pays principle and sustainable development. Its decisions can be appealed in the Supreme Court within 90 days.
facts: Set up under the National Green Tribunal Act (2010).
India is the third country, after Australia and New Zealand, to set up a specialised environmental tribunal.
Principal seat is in New Delhi; regional benches include Bhopal, Pune and Chennai.
Chairperson: a retired Supreme Court judge or High Court Chief Justice, appointed in consultation with the Chief Justice of India.
Judicial members: 10-20, exact number decided by the Central Government.
Hears civil cases under seven laws; excludes the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 and the Forest Rights Act 2006.
Appeals can be filed in the Supreme Court within 90 days.
Appeals must be disposed of within 6 months of filing.

facts.title: Malaysia and Seychelles Visits
facts.summary: The Prime Minister's visit to Malaysia produced a joint statement covering defence, digital and trade cooperation. Seychelles' President visited India to announce the SESEL joint vision, marking 50 years of diplomatic relations, along with a USD 175 million assistance package. Both visits stress disaster-resilient infrastructure, and the Seychelles visit also stresses maritime security.
facts: India and Malaysia set up a Strategic Affairs Working Group and a Su-30 Forum for air forces
Malaysia-India Digital Council formalised for fintech, AI, cybersecurity and e-governance
RBI and Bank Negara Malaysia to promote local currency settlement
Malaysia is India's 3rd largest trading partner in ASEAN
Harimau Shakti (5th Edition) is a joint military exercise with Malaysia
Malaysia formally acceded to the International Big Cat Alliance
SESEL: Joint Vision for Sustainability, Growth and Security through Enhanced Linkages
India announced a USD 175 million assistance package for Seychelles
Seychelles to become a full member of the Colombo Security Conclave

facts.title: Space and Cyber Security
facts.summary: NASA's MESSENGER data revealed bright streaks across Mercury's surface, and the booklet gives key facts about the planet. The Global CyberPeace Summit 2026 was held in New Delhi.
facts: NASA's MESSENGER data revealed numerous bright streaks scattered across Mercury's surface.
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest planet in the Solar System.
Mercury is the fastest orbiting planet around the Sun.
Mercury is the densest planet after Earth and has no moons or rings.
Key Mercury discoveries: water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters and a large, iron-rich core.
Global CyberPeace Summit 2026 concluded in New Delhi, organised by CyberPeace.
Global Quantum Threat Alliance addresses future cyber risks arising from quantum computing.
CoE on Automotive Cybersecurity focuses on securing connected, autonomous and electric vehicles.
